question: The smaller Oceanic tables of the gap audit of 26 November 2026 (Jackson 1983 Tables 22, 25, 29; Jackson 1986 Table 5; Hughes 2020a Table 3; Hughes 2020b Tables 4.1.6-4.1.7; Blumenfeld 2022b Tables 20, 24; Lynch 2004 Tables 1-3, 9; Lynch 2005b Tables 2-3; Lynch 2019a Tables 3, 5, 7; Lynch 2022 Tables 1-2, 6, 9-11; Lynch & Brotchie 2010 Tables 4-5; Bril 2020; François 2005 Table 4; François 2009 Tables 4, 14; Ellis 2012 Tables 2-2, 2-4, 3-17; Ross 1988 Tables 11-16, 19; Ross et al. 2023 Tables 1.8-1.9): what is entered?
chosen_reading: Two new lects, Shark Bay (lore1244) and Tolomako (tolo1255), with the reflexes of POc *m, *b, *p from Lynch (2005b: 400, Table 3): 12 rows, stated against POc, the lects listed under Northern Vanuatu. Lynch's v is written β for Tolomako; Shark Bay f is kept. Nothing else: the other tables are word lists that illustrate reflexes already entered, reproductions or earlier versions of tables already entered (Jackson 1983 Table 25 = Jackson 1986 Table 1; Ross 1988 Tables 11, 12, 16 = Tables 26-27; Ellis's tables after Quackenbush 1968 and Jackson 1983, 1986; Hughes's tables after Bender et al. 2003a), or summaries above the level of a lect.
alternatives: Enter Ross (1988: 72) Table 14, the reflexes of POc *s (fortis s, lenis z), *c and *j in his proto-languages, for the nodes that exist: Proto-New Ireland (s, c; s; c), Proto-Lavongai/Nalik (s; s; s), Proto-Southeast Solomonic (s, z [ð]; z [ð]; d), Proto-Central Pacific (s, c [ð]; z; j), Proto-Eastern Oceanic (s, z). Held back because the POC > PLN, PMAD rows of Table 34 were held back (decision ross1988-mm), because Ross's 1988 PNI *c is not in the Proto-New Ireland inventory of Ross (1994: 556), and because the PCP and PSS columns restate Geraghty (1986) and others. Enter Lynch (2022: 260) Table 1, the POc vowels in eight Southern Vanuatu languages, composed onto the Lynch (2001) nodes. Compare Hughes (2020b: 176-177) Tables 4.1.6-4.1.7 cell by cell: by lect and proto-phoneme the reflex sets agree with the rows already entered, except that his 'S.Carolinian' has h for *t and n for *n, *ñ and his 'S.C.Tanapag' s and l, the reverse of the rows from Jackson & Marck (1991) and Ellis (2012) (Carolinian s, l; Tanapag h, n). Add Tape (Lynch & Brotchie 2010) and the other Santo languages of Lynch (2019a: 304, Table 4).
